Wayne Thompson, a paleontologist examining the find, called it the most complete and spectacular mastodon molar from the region he has ever encountered, describing the moment as giving him chills.
Pacific mastodons, relatives of modern elephants, roamed the American West for millions of years before vanishing over 10,000 years ago. Their extinction resulted from a combination of climate change affecting their habitat and overhunting by humans. These herbivorous giants once wandered across what is now California, Oregon, the Rocky Mountains, and parts of Mexico. The tooth has been donated to Stanford University, where researchers plan to use carbon dating to pinpoint its exact age and learn more about the ecosystem these creatures inhabited.
This discovery joins a growing collection of mastodon finds that continue to emerge across North America, including a jaw found beneath a New York lawn in 2024 and another tooth discovered on a California beach the year before. As researchers note, fossils like this tooth offer an irreplaceable window into ancient biodiversity, helping scientists understand past ecosystems and make more informed decisions about protecting wildlife today. It's a quiet reminder that traces of vanished worlds still rest beneath our feet, waiting to be found.

item.title: Auckland's City Rail Link stations are a feast for the eyes
item.description:
After a decade of planning and construction, Auckland's new City Rail Link stations have opened as unexpected galleries of Māori art and storytelling. Three underground stations—Karanga-a-Hape, Maungawhau, and Te Waihorotiu—weave together contemporary design and traditional narratives, transforming daily commutes into encounters with the cultural and natural history of Tāmaki Makaurau (Auckland).
Each station tells distinct stories through carefully chosen materials and symbols. At Karanga-a-Hape, artist Reuben Kirkwood carved lunar phases into ancient heart kauri, creating "Me te Ōturu" to reflect the Māori lunar calendar and its connection to tides and celestial rhythms. Sculptural pūpūrangi (kauri snail) shells nearby honor the relationship between people and nature. Te Waihorotiu Station features over 4,000 golden rods representing raupō reeds that once grew in the now-buried Waihorotiu Stream, while seven skylights evoke the stars of Matariki. Hidden within this metal forest is a kauri carving of Horotiu, a serpent-like guardian spirit. At Maungawhau Station, Tessa Harris designed a dramatic waterwall combining basalt, concrete, and glass to tell the story of freshwater and volcanic deities, with 53 glass triangles mapping Auckland's volcanic cones in colors that evoke molten lava.
What makes this project quietly remarkable is its commitment to making infrastructure meaningful. Rather than treating public transit stations as purely functional spaces, Auckland has created places where thousands of daily travelers can connect with ancestral stories, geological time, and the living landscape beneath their feet—a reminder that even underground, we move through layers of history and belonging.

item.title: Why we have warm blood and what advantages it has over cold blood
item.description:
Why do humans maintain a steady body temperature of around 37 degrees Celsius, whether shivering in Antarctica or sweating in the Sahara? This question leads to a fascinating exploration of warm-blooded versus cold-blooded animals, and the evolutionary journey that separates them. The terms themselves—"cold-blooded" and "warm-blooded"—are somewhat misleading. Cold-blooded animals, or ectotherms, regulate their temperature externally, relying on their environment. Warm-blooded creatures, or endotherms, generate heat internally. A desert lizard basking in the sun can actually be warmer than many mammals, making the labels relative rather than absolute.
The language of "cold blood" has curious roots in ancient Greek medicine, particularly the Theory of Humors proposed by Hipocrates and Galen. They believed bodily fluids controlled temperament, and that blood literally heated up during strong emotions—hence expressions like "blood boiling." Writers in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries adopted this medical metaphor to describe human behavior, coining phrases like acting "in cold blood" long before scientists formally classified reptiles and amphibians as cold-blooded in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. All animals originally descended from ectothermic fish, but some evolved fur or feathers that enabled them to retain body heat, giving rise to endotherms—still a minority among Earth's creatures.
This story offers a window into how evolution shaped our biology and how ancient medical theories continue to color our everyday language. It's a quiet reminder that understanding our own bodies connects us to both natural history and cultural heritage, revealing the remarkable systems that keep us functioning optimally at a precise temperature.

item.title: Belém fashion show transforms history and architecture into Amazonian fashion pieces
item.description:
In Belém, Brazil, a historic mansion has become an unlikely muse for contemporary fashion. Sixteen original garments, inspired by the architecture, colors, and stories of Casa SESI—a cultural center housed in a traditional Amazonian building—will be unveiled in a public fashion show that blends heritage with creative sustainability.
The collection emerged from a five-day artistic residency that challenged fashion professionals to translate the mansion's physical details and historical memory into wearable art. Participants drew on architectural forms, the building's palette, and decorative elements as creative references. The project also embraced environmental responsibility: designers worked primarily with repurposed materials including jute waste, reclaimed wood, and donated twill fabric from local partner companies. Following the runway presentation, all sixteen pieces will remain on display, allowing visitors to examine the craftsmanship, textures, and innovative material choices up close. The event will also feature a performance by the SESI Sustainable Orchestra, a youth ensemble that plays Amazonian-inspired music on instruments made from recycled and alternative materials.
This story offers a quiet lesson in how cultural heritage and environmental consciousness can inform contemporary creativity. By rooting fashion design in local history and sustainable practice, the project honors both place and resourcefulness. Visitors to the exhibition are invited to contribute clean fabric donations, which will support free sewing and fashion courses serving some 5,000 students each semester—extending the project's impact well beyond the runway. It's a reminder that innovation often flourishes when artists are asked to listen carefully to what already exists around them.

item.title: Audiobooks gain ground among Book Fair readers and help Brazilians fit literature into their routines
item.description:
At Brazil's 28th São Paulo Book Fair, a quieter shift is taking place alongside the crowds hunting for autographs and new releases: audiobooks are finding their place in Brazilian readers' lives. Far from replacing physical books, the audio format is helping people weave literature into moments that would otherwise go unread—commutes, gym sessions, household chores. For student Giovanna Lima Silva, it's a practical complement: she reads physical books at home and listens to audiobooks during her hour-long daily bus rides through crowded São Paulo traffic.
The trend reflects a broader challenge. According to the sixth edition of Brazil's "Portraits of Reading" survey, 75% of readers wish they read more, but 46% cite lack of time as the main barrier. Audiobook adoption is climbing: 23% of Brazilians reported listening to one in 2024, up from 20% in 2019, with the figure reaching 44% among those with higher education. Yet print remains king—83% of readers last engaged with a physical book. Author Bruna Martiolli, who narrated the audiobook version of her own work "It's Strawberry Time," describes the forty-hour recording process as emotionally demanding and says it changed her initial skepticism about the format.
This story offers a window into how technology is quietly expanding access to literature rather than diminishing it. Nearly half of audiobook users report reading significantly more after adopting the format, with an estimated 18 million Brazilians increasing their overall reading through digital books. It's a reminder that innovation doesn't always mean replacement—sometimes it simply means finding new pathways to old pleasures.
